passage:
The village youth club had a plan: paint the bus shelter blue for the fair. Rajni, the group's leader, had already ordered the paint. Neelam sat cross-legged on the floor, chewing the corner of her dupatta. She knew the rain would wash ordinary paint off within a week; her uncle had told her so about the tank wall. But Rajni was her friend, and everyone else was nodding. Neelam felt hot, torn between loyalty and honesty.

“Rajni,” she finally said, “can I say something? I think the paint will wash away. Maybe the weatherproof kind?” The room went quiet. Rajni frowned, then asked, “How much more is it?” “I can find out from the shop tomorrow,” said Neelam. Rajni nodded slowly. “Okay. Find out.”

qa.a: Rajni had already ordered the paint.

qa.q: Why did Neelam feel hot, torn between loyalty and honesty?
qa.a: Neelam valued Rajni's friendship and did not want to break the nodding, yet believed the paint would wash away.

qa.q: What small step did Neelam offer after speaking up?
qa.a: Neelam offered to find out the price of the weatherproof paint from the shop the next day.

qa.q: What might Rajni have felt when Neelam spoke up in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rajni may have felt surprised and briefly defensive, having already ordered the paint, but was willing to listen.

grounding: A teenager in a group disagrees with a decision, feels torn between loyalty and speaking up, and offers an honest contribution.

passage:
The student council at a Birmingham school was planning a fundraiser. Kwame, the president, said, “Bake sale on Friday, done.” Everyone nodded. Selin's stomach twisted. Half the year group would be at mock exams on Friday. She had said yes to the last three ideas because Kwame was a friend and worked hard. Her pen tapped the table. Silent agreement was easier, she thought, but it wouldn't help him.

“Kwame,” she said, “I like the bake sale, but Friday is mock exam day. Could we do Thursday?” Two people looked up with relief. Kwame paused, then grinned a little awkwardly. “Okay. I hadn't checked. Thursday.”

qa.a: Kwame said, “Bake sale on Friday, done.”

qa.q: Why did Selin not speak up on the last three ideas?
qa.a: Selin valued Kwame as a friend and saw how hard Kwame worked, so agreeing felt easier and kinder.

qa.q: What choice did Selin make when Kwame announced Friday?
qa.a: Selin said she liked the bake sale but pointed out the mock exam clash and suggested Thursday.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt when Selin questioned Friday?
qa.a: Kwame probably felt a little embarrassed at not checking, but relieved that the problem was found before the event.

grounding: A teenager in a group disagrees with a decision, feels torn between loyalty and speaking up, and gives honest input.
